title: The Holy Innocents (28 December)
hook: Herod's massacre remembered; a day for all children who suffer

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saint Stephen, in red the day after Christmas. Your line was the crib and the cross. Did you get to your kindness for someone poor? Day six hundred forty-two.

There's a carol from Coventry, in England, that sounds like a lullaby. It's soft and slow, and it's sung by mothers to their babies. Then you listen to the words, and you realize the mothers are singing because soldiers are coming. It's from a medieval play about this day. Three days after Christmas, the Church remembers the darkest scene in the whole infancy story, one that nativity sets leave out. It belongs to the season anyway: Matthew tells it in the same chapter as the star.
screen: `A LULLABY FROM COVENTRY.` → `SOLDIERS ARE COMING.` → `THE SCENE THE CRIBS LEAVE OUT.`

segments.voice: In Matthew's gospel, the magi stop in Jerusalem asking where the newborn king of the Jews is. King Herod, who has a long record of killing anyone he sees as a rival, asks them to report back. They don't. They go home another way. Joseph, warned in a dream, takes Mary and the child by night and flees to Egypt. And Herod, furious, sends soldiers to kill every boy in Bethlehem and its borders two years old and under. Matthew then reaches back to the prophet Jeremiah. In the Douay-Rheims: "Rachel bewailing her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." Rachel, the wife of Jacob, was buried by tradition on the road near Bethlehem. Jeremiah had pictured her weeping over her people carried into exile. Matthew hears her weeping again. An honest note: no other ancient source records this massacre. The historian Josephus describes Herod's cruelty at length, including the killing of his own sons, but not this. Bethlehem was a small village, and many scholars think the number of children would have been small too, perhaps a dozen or two, though later legends grew it into thousands. The Church honors these children as martyrs. Not because they chose to die for Christ, but because they died in his place, too young to say a word. And so the day has become a day for every child who suffers from the violence of the powerful: in war, in hunger, in flight, in danger at home. The Holy Family themselves end this story as refugees.
screen: `THE MAGI GO HOME ANOTHER WAY.` · `THE FLIGHT INTO EGYPT.` · `RACHEL WEEPING.` · `NO OTHER SOURCE, AND A SMALL TOWN.` · then, large: `SHE WOULD NOT BE COMFORTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold children in danger. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind children you know of who are not safe tonight: in a war zone you've seen on the news, in a shelter, in a hospital, in a hard home down the street. Don't look away from them, and don't try to fix it in two minutes. Just let them be real to you, one at a time. If you pray, you can pray for them by name or by place. If you don't, let your attention be a kind of keeping watch. The bell holds the time.
Herod, the king. Matthew's gospel: in his fury at the magi's escape, he sent soldiers to kill the children of Bethlehem, honored on December 28. Today's word.
Your line: rachel weeping. Today, find one way to help a child in danger: a gift to a charity, a call, a question to someone who works with kids. Day six hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics keep December 28 as the feast of the Holy Innocents, and many parishes and families use it to pray for children who suffer, including the unborn, refugees and children in war.

original.note: Hebrew: Rachel weeping for her children, Jeremiah 31:15 (31:14 in Hebrew Bibles).

trapdoor: what you thought: a gruesome footnote to Christmas.
what it means: the children Herod killed, honored as martyrs, and a day for all children who suffer.
what a scholar hears: Matthew alone tells it; Josephus is silent, though he records Herod killing his own sons, and Matthew reads it through Jeremiah 31:15.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 2:18 (quoted only from 'Rachel bewailing').
Scholarly estimates of the number of children (often 'a dozen or two', sometimes fewer) and later liturgical figures (e.g. 14,000 in Byzantine tradition) are given generally; confirm.
Josephus records Herod's execution of his sons Alexander, Aristobulus and Antipater; confirm the reference.
The Coventry Carol comes from the Pageant of the Shearmen and Tailors (Coventry mystery plays). Confirm.
Many parishes connect the day to the unborn; included only in howItsDone. Keeper may adjust.
